title: Carbide-free mangoes: how hay ripening works and how to check
summary: How mangoes ripen, why calcium carbide is banned for ripening, how hay ripening works, and how to ripen and store Kesar mangoes at home.
body:
Every summer in India, food-safety officials seize mangoes ripened with calcium carbide. If you have wondered what that means, what "hay-ripened" mangoes are, and how to tell the difference at the fruit stall, this guide is for you.

## How a mango ripens

Mangoes are what botanists call climacteric fruit: they keep ripening after they are picked. A mature mango gives off ethylene, a plant hormone, which sets off the changes we call ripening:

- starch in the flesh turns to sugar, so the fruit gets sweeter;
- the flesh softens and turns from pale cream to deep yellow or orange;
- the skin loses some of its green as chlorophyll breaks down;
- the fruit develops its aroma.

The key word is **mature**. A mango picked when it has reached full size and its flesh has started to colour near the stone will ripen well off the tree. One picked too early never ripens properly, however it is treated.

## What calcium carbide ripening is

Calcium carbide is an industrial chemical used to make acetylene gas, for welding among other things. When it meets moisture it releases acetylene, which acts on fruit somewhat like ethylene. Some traders put packets of carbide among boxes of mangoes to make them colour quickly and all at once, sometimes using fruit that was picked before it was mature.

FSSAI, India's food regulator, prohibits the use of calcium carbide for ripening fruit, under the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011. FSSAI has also warned that industrial-grade carbide can carry traces of arsenic and phosphorus. It reissues advisories to traders and fruit handlers most mango seasons.

FSSAI does permit ripening with ethylene gas in controlled ripening chambers. So "artificially ripened" is not automatically the same as "carbide-ripened". The problem is carbide.

## How hay ripening works

Hay ripening is the old-style way mangoes have been ripened in Indian homes and orchards for generations. Mature mangoes are laid in layers on and between dry hay or paddy straw, in a basket, crate or a cool, closed room. The straw:

- cushions the fruit so it doesn't bruise;
- keeps the fruit a little warmer and holds in humidity;
- traps the ethylene the mangoes give off themselves, so they ripen each other.

Nothing is added. The fruit is checked every day or so, and ripe mangoes are taken out as they are ready, so a batch ripens over several days rather than all at once. How long it takes depends on how mature the fruit was and on the weather.

## How to spot carbide-ripened mangoes

No home test is conclusive, but these signs are worth noticing:

- **Colour**: hay-ripened mangoes often ripen unevenly, with patches of green and yellow. A whole box of uniformly bright yellow mangoes, all ripe on the same day, is a warning sign.
- **Inside vs outside**: carbide can colour the skin faster than the flesh ripens. Yellow skin with pale, hard or sour flesh near the stone is a common giveaway.
- **Smell**: a ripe mango smells sweet and fruity at the stem end. No smell, or a sharp, odd smell, is not a good sign.
- **Feel**: a ripe mango gives slightly when pressed gently near the stem, and the flesh is soft right up to the stone.
- **Residue**: greyish-white powder on the skin or in the box may be carbide residue. Don't buy that fruit.

You may also see "drop it in water and see if it floats" suggested online. Whether a mango floats depends on its size and ripeness, so it doesn't tell you how it was ripened.

## How to ripen Kesar mangoes at home

Kesar is a mango variety best known from Gujarat's Saurashtra region and widely grown in Maharashtra too. It has saffron-coloured flesh (kesar means saffron) and a strong aroma. If your mangoes arrive firm:

- Keep them at room temperature, out of direct sun, in a single layer.
- To speed things up, wrap them loosely in newspaper or put them in a paper bag, or bury them in a basket of straw or uncooked rice, as many Indian households do.
- Check every day. They are ready when they smell sweet at the stem end and give slightly to a gentle press.
- Don't refrigerate unripe mangoes. Cold stops them ripening properly.

## How to store ripe mangoes

Once ripe, refrigerate them and eat them within 2–3 days. Many households soak mangoes in a bowl of water for 30 minutes to an hour before eating. It washes the skin and loosens the sticky sap at the stem end. Always wash the skin before you cut the fruit.
